question_bank.stem: A single prompt both extracts issues from a customer review and writes the final response, but you cannot tell where errors come from. What redesign best matches the lecture?

options.text: Keep the single prompt and add more adjectives so the model has a stronger stylistic signal.
Collapse the workflow further by removing the extraction step and asking only for the final email.
Replace the workflow with one longer context window so intermediate reasoning never needs to be externalized.
Split the workflow into chained prompts so extraction, outlining, and final writing can each be inspected separately.

question_bank.rationale: The lecture defines chaining as splitting a complex workflow into multiple prompts whose intermediate outputs can be debugged independently.

source_ref.evidence_span: So one advantage of chaining is you would separate the prompts,

frame_evidence.visual_description: Slide titled Chain complex prompts for improved performance contrasts a single-step customer-response prompt with a multi-prompt decomposition.

question_bank.stem: You want to know whether poor email quality comes from issue extraction, outline generation, or final writing. Which diagnostic benefit of chaining did the lecture emphasize?

options.text: You can test the prompts separately and optimize the weakest step instead of guessing which hidden subtask failed.
You can eliminate intermediate outputs so the model has fewer chances to expose errors during evaluation.
You can force all three subtasks to share the same hidden state so debugging is no longer needed.
You can guarantee that every later prompt is correct as long as the first prompt produces any output at all.

question_bank.rationale: The lecture says chained prompts can be tested independently, which makes it easier to identify which step should be optimized.

source_ref.evidence_span: test those three prompts separately from each other

frame_evidence.visual_description: Chaining slide remains visible while the instructor points to the separated extraction, outline, and final-response stages.

question_bank.stem: A team proposes a very long chain for a chatbot that must answer almost instantly. Which caution from the lecture is most relevant?

options.text: Longer chains reduce latency because every extra prompt shortens the model's decoding path.
Longer chains can improve control, but they also add latency that may be unacceptable in speed-sensitive applications.
Longer chains remove the need for intermediate evaluation because later prompts automatically correct earlier ones.
Longer chains make prompt engineering unnecessary because the workflow logic replaces prompt quality.

question_bank.rationale: The lecture notes that chained workflows help control and debugging, but longer chains can be undesirable when latency matters.

frame_evidence.visual_description: The slide and narration focus on why multi-step control improves debugging even though it may cost additional model calls.

question_bank.stem: You are comparing a baseline prompt against a refined prompt across several test cases. What evaluation setup most closely matches the lecture's prompt-testing advice?

options.text: Judge the prompts only by how elegant they look before execution, because wording quality predicts output quality.
Measure only token count, because shorter prompts are usually the stronger prompts across tasks.
Run both prompts on representative cases, inspect the generated outputs, and score the results side by side.
Pick the prompt that sounds more confident, because confidence is the main indicator of a reliable workflow.

question_bank.rationale: Prompt testing in the lecture compares baseline and refined prompts on actual cases and reviews their generated outputs.

frame_evidence.visual_description: Slide titled Testing your prompts shows a table with prompt variants, test cases, generated outputs, and scores.

question_bank.stem: You already have a reference answer and want an automated evaluator to compare two model outputs against it. Which judge pattern from the lecture is the best fit?

options.text: Use a zero-shot generator as the final answerer, because generation and judging should be the same step.
Use a chain-of-thought prompt only, because reference answers are unnecessary once the model reasons step by step.
Use a single-answer grader with no comparison or rubric, because pairwise judgments become invalid when a reference exists.
Use a reference-guided LLM judge that compares both candidate answers against the provided reference.

question_bank.rationale: The lecture presents several judge modes, including reference-guided pairwise comparison when a reference answer is available.

source_ref.evidence_span: Or you add also a rubric.

frame_evidence.visual_description: Slide titled LLM as Judges shows pairwise, single-answer, and reference-guided judging prompts alongside rubric-style evaluation.
